original_question: Suppose that a billiard table has a sequence of convex caustics with rotation numbers converging to some number ω ∈ (0, 1/2). Does it imply that the table is an ellipse?
target_in_paper: Question 3.10 in Section 3.2.2, "Geometry of caustics, invariant surfaces, and commuting billiard maps." The paper poses exactly the question your draft is aiming at: "Suppose that a billiard table has a sequence of convex caustics with rotation numbers converging to some number ω ∈ (0, 1/2). Does it imply that the table is an ellipse?" It is introduced as "a variation on Innami’s result" and is said to be suggested by V. Kaloshin. ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the exact logical core of the paper’s Question 3.10 almost verbatim: the existence of a sequence of convex caustics, convergence of their rotation numbers to some ω in (0,1/2), and the conclusion asking whether the billiard table must be an ellipse. ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))
missing_details: The ambient setting is the planar inner billiard: the paper’s standing setup is a smooth strictly convex domain Ω ⊂ R^2 bounded by a smooth curve γ. Without saying this, the question is not fully stand-alone. ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))

The term "caustic" is used in the standard planar billiard sense from Section 3.2: in dimension two, an invariant curve of the billiard map has an envelope, and that envelope is called a billiard caustic. The refined question should make clear that the sequence consists of billiard caustics for the inner billiard in Ω. ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))

The phrase "rotation numbers" refers to the rotation numbers of the corresponding invariant circles of the billiard map. The nearby subsection explains rotation numbers through invariant circles, especially for p/q-rational caustics. ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))

The conclusion should be stated as a property of the boundary: namely, whether ∂Ω (equivalently the billiard curve γ) must be an ellipse. ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))

To remain paper-faithful, the question should stay as Question 3.10 and not be broadened to the stronger neighboring Conjecture 3.9, which assumes a whole family of rotational invariant circles for every rotation number in (0,1/2). ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))

No ambient ring/field, homogeneity, degree, nilpotency, or "for all sufficiently large m" type quantifiers are relevant here; the omitted information is geometric and dynamical, not algebraic. ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))
refined_question: Let Ω ⊂ R^2 be a smooth strictly convex planar billiard table, with inner billiard map defined by specular reflection at ∂Ω. Suppose that Ω admits a sequence of convex billiard caustics C_n whose corresponding invariant circles have rotation numbers ρ_n converging to some ω ∈ (0,1/2). Must the boundary ∂Ω be an ellipse? ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))
justification: The draft clearly targets Section 3.2.2, Question 3.10, not a broader neighboring problem. It matches the paper’s official wording essentially word-for-word. The surrounding context shows how to sharpen it without changing its scope: Section 3.2 provides the planar smooth strictly convex billiard setup and defines caustics via invariant curves, while the immediately preceding paragraph in Section 3.2.2 explains rotation numbers in terms of invariant circles. The paper also explicitly positions Question 3.10 as a weaker variation on Innami’s theorem and as distinct from the stronger Conjecture 3.9. Therefore the right refinement is to make the planar inner-billiard setting and the dynamical meaning of caustic/rotation number explicit, while keeping the exact hypothesis and conclusion of Question 3.10 unchanged in substance. ([upcommons.upc.edu](https://upcommons.upc.edu/bitstreams/d858abf8-e232-45e3-a199-3adac6cf7893/download))
